title: Fresnel Diffraction
short_intro: Fresnel diffraction is a class of diffraction phenomena occurring when the source of light, the obstacle or aperture, and the screen are at finite distances from one another, such that the incident and diffracted wavefronts are spherical or cylindrical. It utilizes the concept of Fresnel half-period zones to analyze intensity variations.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of wavefront division, distinction between Fresnel and Fraunhofer diffraction, diffraction at a straight edge, circular aperture, and narrow wire using zone plates.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Analytical treatment of half-period zones, radius of Fresnel zones, intensity at a point due to a wavefront, zone plate construction, theory, and focal lengths.

prerequisites: Superposition of waves and phase interference
Geometry of spherical and plane wavefronts

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Wavefront Geometry
bullets: In Fresnel diffraction, either the source of light or the observation screen or both are at a finite distance from the aperture or obstacle.
The wavefronts arriving at the obstacle and traveling toward the screen are spherical or cylindrical rather than planar.
No lenses are required to focus the rays; observations are made in the near field relative to the aperture.

concept_notes.heading: Fresnel Half-Period Zones (HPZs)
bullets: A wavefront can be divided into concentric annular regions called half-period zones such that the path difference from any two corresponding points in consecutive zones to the observation point is lambda/2.
The phase difference between disturbances arriving from consecutive zones at the observation point is pi radians (out of phase).
The resultant amplitude at the observation point is given by the alternating series R = m1 - m2 + m3 - m4 + ... where amplitudes m decrease slowly as the zone number increases.

concept_notes.heading: Zone Plate
bullets: A zone plate is a special screen designed to obstruct alternate Fresnel zones (e.g., even zones), acting somewhat like a convex lens with multiple foci.
The radius of the n-th Fresnel zone is proportional to the square root of n: r_n proportional to sqrt(n).
Unlike a glass lens, a zone plate has multiple focal lengths given by f_n = r_1^2 / (n \lambda), producing numerous chromatic foci.

concept_notes.heading: Comparison with Fraunhofer Diffraction
bullets: Fresnel class involves finite source-aperture and aperture-screen distances; Fraunhofer class involves infinite distances.
Fresnel diffraction patterns scale with distance and have curved wavefronts; Fraunhofer patterns are independent of distance in scale factor and use lenses to render wavefronts plane.
Mathematical treatment of Fresnel diffraction involves Fresnel integrals and Cornu's spiral.

derivations.title: Radius of n-th Fresnel Half-Period Zone
derivations.conditions: Point source S at distance a from wavefront, observation point P at distance b from wavefront.
steps: Let S be a point source and P be the point of observation at a distance (a + b) from S.
Consider a spherical wavefront with center S and radius a passing through O. Let M_n be the outer boundary of the n-th half-period zone on the wavefront.
The distance from S to the n-th zone point M_n is SM_n = a, and the distance from M_n to P is M_n_P = b + n\lambda/2 by definition of half-period zones.
Using geometry in triangle SM_nP, if r_n is the radius of the n-th zone, expanding using binomial approximation yields r_n^2 \approx \frac{a b}{a + b} n \lambda.
Therefore, the radius of the n-th zone is r_n = \sqrt{\frac{a b}{a + b} n \lambda}.

derivations.title: Focal Length of a Zone Plate
derivations.conditions: Normal incidence of monochromatic light of wavelength lambda on a zone plate of radius r_n for the n-th zone.
steps: The phase condition for constructive interference at the focus F at distance f from the zone plate requires the path difference from the n-th zone to be n\lambda/2.
The distance from the n-th zone boundary to the focus F is \sqrt{f^2 + r_n^2}.
Equating the total path from the source to focus via the n-th zone: \sqrt{f^2 + r_n^2} - f = n\lambda/2.
Using the expression for the radius of the n-th zone where a approaches infinity (plane wavefront), r_n^2 = n \lambda f_1, substitute into the binomial expansion.
Solving for focal length f yields f = \frac{r_n^2}{n \lambda} = f_1 / n, where f_1 is the principal focal length.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Cornu's Spiral
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A clothoid or Cornu's spiral plotting Fresnel integrals C(v) on the x-axis and S(v) on the y-axis, spiraling symmetrically toward asymptotic points (0.5, 0.5) and (-0.5, -0.5).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used to graphically compute amplitude and phase of diffracted light in Fresnel diffraction problems by measuring vector lengths on the spiral.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually for finding intensity distributions near sharp edges and obstacles.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Intensity Distribution at a Straight Edge
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph of intensity versus distance on the screen, showing damped oscillations inside the geometrical shadow and a series of maxima and minima outside the geometrical shadow.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates light bleeding into the shadow region and finite interference fringes near the edge boundary due to Fresnel diffraction.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Distinguishing Fresnel diffraction at an edge from rectilinear propagation of light.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Zone Plate Focus Intensity Profile
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Intensity peaks corresponding to primary, secondary, and higher-order foci along the optical axis behind a zone plate.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows multiple focal points (f, f/3, f/5, etc.) because a zone plate acts simultaneously as a converging and diverging lens element.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Comparison questions between glass lenses and zone plates.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the radius of the first half-period zone of a zone plate for light of wavelength 5000 Å, given that the source is at infinity and the screen is at a distance of 1 m.
solution_steps: Identify given values: lambda = 5000 Å = 5 * 10^-7 m, a = infinity (so a/(a+b) -> 1), b = 1 m, n = 1.
Use the formula for zone radius: r_n = \sqrt{b n \lambda}.
Calculate the value: r_1 = \sqrt{5 	imes 10^{-7}} = \sqrt{50 	imes 10^{-8}} = 7.07 \times 10^{-4} m.

solved_numericals.question: A zone plate has a diameter of 1.2 cm for the 10th zone. If light of wavelength 6000 Å falls normally on it, find the principal focal length of the zone plate.
solution_steps: Identify given values: Diameter 2r_10 = 1.2 cm = 0.012 m, so r_10 = 0.6 cm = 0.006 m.
Number of the zone n = 10, wavelength lambda = 6000 Å = 6 * 10^-7 m.
Use the formula for focal length: f_n = \frac{r_n^2}{n \lambda}.

solved_numericals.question: Find the radius of the third half-period zone of a wavefront of wavelength 589 nm, when the distance from the point source to the wavefront is 2 m and the distance from the wavefront to the observation point is 3 m.
solution_steps: Identify given values: a = 2 m, b = 3 m, n = 3, lambda = 589 nm = 589 * 10^-9 m.
Use the zone radius formula: r_n = \sqrt{\frac{a b}{a + b} n \lambda}.
Calculate the distance factor: \frac{a b}{a + b} = \frac{2 \times 3}{2 + 3} = \frac{6}{5} = 1.2 m.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes scalar wave approximation where polarization effects of light are ignored.
Assumes the obliquity factor (1 + cos theta) varies slowly and can be approximated across small zones.
Limited to near-field conditions where source-aperture and aperture-screen distances are finite.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Fresnel diffraction requires lenses to observe patterns.
common_misconceptions.correct: Fresnel diffraction occurs at finite distances without lenses; lenses are used in Fraunhofer diffraction.
common_misconceptions.why: Lenses are employed to render wavefronts planar in Fraunhofer setups, whereas Fresnel deals directly with spherical/cylindrical wavefronts.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A zone plate has only one focal point like a convex lens.
common_misconceptions.correct: A zone plate has multiple focal points corresponding to different odd integers (f, f/3, f/5, etc.).
common_misconceptions.why: Higher order diffraction orders constructively interfere at multiple axial positions due to zone boundary phase conditions.

quick_revision: Fresnel diffraction involves finite source-to-screen distances with spherical or cylindrical wavefronts.
Half-period zones divide the wavefront with consecutive path differences of lambda/2.
Radius of n-th Fresnel zone is proportional to the square root of n.
A zone plate acts as a converging lens with multiple foci and chromatic aberration.
